proof:
Source. Step 6 of the parent proof (unit orientations a.e. on M′), separated from its use. The parent applies it with:
- m := n, d := n + 1 and its own B;
- B′ := B ∩ B_{δ₁/2}(0), G(y) := x + ιy + u(y), and the Jacobian J from area_formula;
- p(v) := '0 < J(v) and J(v)^{-1}ξ̃(v) is a unit orientation of some subspace'.
Notation. H^m := μHE[m]. ℝ^d and ℝ^P carry their Borel σ-algebras.
1. (The exceptional set.)
- B is Borel, so H^m⌞B(N) = H^m(N ∩ B) for every set N (Measure.restrict_apply'). So the hypothesis on p says H^m({v : ¬p(v)} ∩ B) = 0 (ae_iff).
- Choose a Borel T ⊇ {v : ¬p(v)} ∩ B with H^m(T) = 0 (exists_measurable_superset_of_null), and put S := T ∩ B.
- Then S is Borel, S ⊆ B and H^m(S) = 0 (measure_mono_null). Every v ∈ B with ¬p(v) lies in S.
2. (Borel images.) ℝ^d is Polish. S and B′ are Borel subsets of B, and G is continuous and injective on each of them, by restricting the hypotheses on B. By the Lusin–Souslin theorem (MeasurableSet.image_of_continuousOn_injOn), G(S) and G(B′) are Borel.
3. (G(S) is null.) Apply the area formula to g := 1_{G(S)}.
- Left side. G(S) is Borel and G(S) ⊆ G(B), so ∫⁻_{G(B)} 1_{G(S)} dH^m = H^m⌞G(B)(G(S)) = H^m(G(S) ∩ G(B)) = H^m(G(S)) (lintegral_indicator_one, Measure.restrict_apply).
- Right side, pointwise. Let v ∈ B with v ∉ S. Suppose G(v) ∈ G(S), say G(v′) = G(v) with v′ ∈ S ⊆ B. Then v′ = v by injectivity of G on B, so v ∈ S, a contradiction. Hence 1_{G(S)}(G(v)) = 0 and ofReal(J(v))·1_{G(S)}(G(v)) = 0.
- Since H^m(S) = 0, H^m-a.e. v ∉ S (measure_eq_zero_iff_ae_notMem), hence H^m⌞B-a.e. v ∉ S (ae_restrict_of_ae). Also H^m⌞B-a.e. v ∈ B (ae_restrict_mem).
- So the integrand vanishes H^m⌞B-a.e., and the right side is 0 (lintegral_congr_ae, lintegral_zero). Therefore H^m(G(S)) = 0.
4. (Conclusion.) Because G(B′) is Borel, it suffices to show the following (ae_restrict_iff'): for H^m-a.e. w, if w ∈ G(B′) then some v ∈ B′ has G(v) = w and p(v).
- By step 3, H^m-a.e. w satisfies w ∉ G(S) (measure_eq_zero_iff_ae_notMem). Take such a w with w ∈ G(B′), and write w = G(v) with v ∈ B′.
- Suppose ¬p(v). Then v ∈ B (as B′ ⊆ B), so v ∈ T by the choice of T, hence v ∈ S. Then w = G(v) ∈ G(S), a contradiction.
- Hence p(v), and v is the required point. ∎
key_steps: The hypothesis gives H^m({¬p} ∩ B) = 0. Enlarge this to a Borel null set S = T ∩ B ⊆ B containing every v ∈ B with ¬p(v).
G(S) and G(B′) are Borel by Lusin–Souslin, since G is continuous and injective on B.
The area formula with g = 1_{G(S)}, together with G(v) ∈ G(S) ⇔ v ∈ S for v ∈ B, gives H^m(G(S)) = ∫⁻_B ofReal(J)·1_S dH^m = 0.
Outside the null set G(S), each w = G(v) ∈ G(B′) has v ∉ S, hence p(v).
